name: Pedro Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a three-man crew for Kerrigan Build, a local contractor doing decks, fences, garden rooms and small single-storey extensions out in the suburbs. I'm the junior, so I dig post holes, mix concrete, carry the timber round the side of people's houses and cut the deck boards once Liam (the lead carpenter) has set out. Every garden's different, every customer's different, and I like that. What wears me out is the digging in clay.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What about life outside, and how you got here?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My dad was a bricklayer, and I left school at sixteen to labour with him, then did my trade certificate later. I live with my girlfriend Ana, who's a hairdresser at her mum's salon, and we've got about three months saved, plus a loan on a little van. On weekends I do my own small jobs, sheds and fences, and I use AI every day for the quotes, the invoices, the material lists and even the adverts. I want my own firm one day, and I don't want anyone handing it to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still a handy tool and people expected too much. I'd tell the lads it does my paperwork in ten minutes, and that's enough for me. I'd probably post a picture of a deck with a joke about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it suits me fine. My job's outdoors and hands-on, people keep wanting garden rooms, and I've got a cheap office assistant on my phone. I'd just keep building up the weekend work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at Kerrigan and learn setting out from Liam. Push the weekend jobs to two a month and save the profit for a second-hand mitre saw and a trailer. Pay the van loan off a year early if I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite good, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the weekend jobs? Does anything change there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit more work, probably. My phone writes a better quote than half the builders in town, and customers think I'm a proper firm. So I'd use that to win a few more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the pressure in your life right now, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The van loan, and rent. Ana and I want to get engaged next year, maybe, and that costs money. But that's normal life. Nothing's going wrong.

I'd tell the lads it does my **paperwork in ten minutes**.
think: My job is **outdoors and hands-on**, and demand for garden rooms holds.
I've got a **cheap office assistant** on my phone already.
do: Learn **setting out** from Liam at Kerrigan.
Grow weekend jobs to **two a month**.
Pay off the **van loan** a year early.

steps.text: Learn setting out from Liam (his lead carpenter) at Kerrigan
Grow weekend shed and fence jobs to two a month
Pay off the van loan a year early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for small firms to punch above their weight. Less red tape, less office staff, more time on the tools. I'd post that, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me. The paperwork side gets even easier, and the big firms lose their edge of having an office full of people. Robots come slowly for garden work, because every garden's a mess of slopes and roots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go harder at the weekend business, maybe set it up properly with a name and insurance. I'd use AI to plan jobs, order materials and answer customer messages. I'd talk to Kerrigan about going part time in a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and pretty excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've already got AI doing your paperwork. What's different in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The customer side, mostly. An AI that answers customer messages at midnight lets a one-man fencing business look as big as a firm with an office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who loses out, in your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Office people at the big builders, estimators, schedulers. I feel for them, but I'd tell them what my dad told me: learn something with your hands. Nobody owes you the job you had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, and don't wait for the government. I'd say small businesses need fewer rules to compete with the robot firms. Online I'd probably be quieter, because people would be angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's tight. By 2028 the thinking side is free for everybody, so my AI advantage disappears. By 2031 big firms have robots that can build a deck, and they'd undercut a one-man band. I'd have three years to get somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full time on my own business by next year, while customers still want a person. I'd save every bit of profit for buying a robot myself once they're affordable, rather than fighting them. I'd keep the van and cut everything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but my brain's already working. It's a race, and I don't like losing races.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ana about the business plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ana (his girlfriend) the engagement ring can wait until we know whether the business survives 2031. She'd be fine. She'd say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be spending money on, or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Spending on the business only, a better saw, a trailer, insurance. Not spending on holidays, the ring or a new phone. Then a robot, if they come down in price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready, so get ready. I'd tell the young lads to start their own thing early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is decent. I'd have the business running properly by 2031, and then three more years before robots hit decks and garden rooms. By 2034 I'd want to be the one renting robots out, or running two of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Kerrigan for a year, then go full time on my own business. I'd save towards a robot or an extra worker. And keep using AI for everything on the paperwork side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, but mostly confident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time give you in the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to build a name. In five years a business with a hundred good reviews is worth more than any robot a big firm can send round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still get engaged?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, next year as we planned. Ana and I don't want to put life on hold for a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty. Build something of your own, and don't sit around waiting for a handout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is great for me. I'd have my own firm with a couple of lads, then add robots when they come in around 2039. I'd be the boss deciding how to use them, not the worker they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, keep going at Kerrigan, grow the weekend work, pay off the van. Then within three years, go full time, hire one lad, and keep learning AI tools as they get better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like I've been given a head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you like to be in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I want a yard, two vans and my own name on the gates, with my dad helping out on Saturdays. Married, maybe a kid. Normal stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could go wrong over that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Recession, mainly. Garden rooms are a nice-to-have, so when money's tight they're the first thing people cancel. That worries me more than robots in this version.

I'd be **the boss** deciding how to use robots around 2039.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one. Two years is no time to build a business before the big firms get robots. The robots won't scare me if they're mine, but they'll finish me if they belong to a big firm first. What would help is less red tape for small firms and cheap loans to buy kit.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how many young lads want their own firm. We're not all waiting for a job. Some of us want to be the ones hiring.

headlineQuote: The robots won't scare me if they're mine, but they'll finish me if they belong to a big firm first.
portrait: Pedro is a 27-year-old **junior** on a small crew building decks, fences and garden rooms.
He lives with **Ana**, a hairdresser, and has three months saved plus a **van loan**.
He uses AI **daily** for quotes and adverts on his weekend side business.
He's **free-market** minded, wanting less red tape and no handouts.
He's anxious with **AGI by 2028**, but plans to own robots rather than fight them.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when big firms get robots before his business is established.
whatWouldHelp: Less **red tape** for small firms and **cheap loans** to buy kit.
